newsitem.title: UK: Hague frontrunner in UK Conservative race.
newsitem.headline: Hague frontrunner in UK Conservative race.

text.p: William Hague, a 36-year-old who promises the Conservatives a fresh start after their election drubbing, on Saturday headed the field to be the next leader of Britain's main opposition party.

Bookmakers have installed the balding politician as favourite to win the six-horse race to replace John Major, who stepped down after the Conservatives plummeted to their worst electoral defeat since 1832.

A Gallup poll for the Sunday Telegraph newspaper showed that Hague, who was Welsh Secretary in the Conservative government, had the most electoral appeal for the demoralised party, struggling to regroup after its defeat by Labour's Tony Blair.
Hague, still remembered for a storming speech at a Conservative conference while still in his teens, has had a meteoric rise in party.
The Sunday Express said supporters of the pro-European former finance minister Kenneth Clarke were ready to switch to Hague in the final stages of the contest which is expected early this summer.
Influential former party manager Tristan Garel-Jones, who played a key role in former prime minister Margaret Thatcher's downfall when she was dumped by the party in 1990, endorsed Hague.
"He is one of the best-equipped all-round politicians to have emerged in the past 20 years, sane, pragmatic and witty," he wrote in the Sunday Express.
Six former cabinet ministers are battling to head the much reduced Conservative force in the House of Commons. Only the party's 164 members of parliament can vote.
Fresh from its landslide victory, Labour has pledged a fresh start in Britain's relations with the European Union, bedevilled during 18 years of Conservative rule.

The winner of the Conservative contest faces an uphill battle to reunite a party rocked by "Eurosceptics" who fear Brussels is eroding national sovereignty and moving towards the establishment of a United States of Europe.
Hague had originally agreed to stand as deputy leader to former interior minister Michael Howard on what would have been a dream ticket. But he pulled out at the last moment and decided to run alone.
"The Conservative Party has got to recover its self-belief and its will to win," said Hague who conceded that his party should learn from Labour's masterly communication skills.
The race to succeed Major was thrown wide open when his deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine pulled out after suffering a recurrence of heart problems.
John Redwood, who challenged Major for the leadership unsuccessfully in 1995, is trying once again. He ranks as one of the most voluble Eurosceptics in parliament.
The other candidates are former social security secretary Peter Lilley and former health secretary Stephen Dorrell.
